paragraphs.source_en: “After that, he consulted with me and said, ‘It seems that slug soup and frog meat are things we cannot get to eat even if we want them, so let us compromise with a Tochimenbo.’ At the time I answered absent-mindedly, ‘That would be fine too.’” The master said, “Hm, this ‘Tochimenbo’ is a strange thing to ask for.” “Yes, it was extremely strange. But Mr. Meitei spoke so earnestly that I was completely taken in.” The visitor seemed to be apologizing to the master for his own carelessness. The master showed no sympathy for the visitor’s apology and indifferently continued, “And then?” “Then Mr. Meitei said to the waiter, ‘Here! Bring us two portions of Tochimenbo,’ and the waiter asked again, ‘Do you mean Menchibo?’ Mr. Meitei, even more solemn than before, said, ‘Not Menchibo. What I want is Tochimenbo.’” The master pressed him eagerly, “Ah. But does such a dish as Tochimenbo really exist?” “Well, I thought it was a little odd too, but Mr. Meitei was so composed, and besides he is such an authority on the West, and at that moment I fully believed he had really been abroad, so I even helped him by telling the waiter, ‘It is Tochimenbo, Tochimenbo.’” “And what did the waiter do then?” “That waiter, when I think of it now, was truly comic. He first pondered for a while and then said, ‘I am terribly sorry, but unfortunately we have no Tochimenbo today. If it is Menchibo you want, we can prepare two portions at once.’ Mr. Meitei looked extremely disappointed, took out a twenty-sen tip for the waiter, and said, ‘If that is so, have we not come all this way for nothing? Could you not contrive some way to let us eat Tochimenbo?’ The waiter said, ‘Then let me go and consult with the cook.’ With that, he went to the back.” The master said teasingly, “It seems this gentleman truly did want to eat Tochimenbo.” “After a while the waiter came out and said, ‘It is most unfortunate; we have none ready-made. If you wish to order the dish, we can prepare it now, but it will take some time.’ Mr. Meitei said calmly, ‘In any case, during the New Year holidays we have nothing to do, so let us wait a little and eat before we go.’ As he said this he took a cigar from his pocket and began puffing at it; having no choice, I too took out the Nihon newspaper and began to read. So the waiter went back again to consult.” With the eagerness he showed when reading war dispatches, the master leaned forward and said, “That is quite a lot of trouble!” “Before long the waiter came out again and, looking deeply apologetic, said, ‘Lately the ingredients for Tochimenbo have been out of stock; even if one goes to Kameya or to No. 15 in Yokohama, they cannot be bought, so we cannot make it.’ Mr. Meitei said, ‘That is a real difficulty. After making such a special trip to eat it, and yet...’ Looking at me, he kept repeating this, and since I could hardly remain silent, I chimed in, ‘It is truly regrettable, truly regrettable.’”

paragraphs.source_en: The master said approvingly, “Quite right.” As for me, I could not understand what was right about it. “Then the waiter, seeming sorry as well, said, ‘When the ingredients come in before long, please do visit us again.’ At that, Mr. Meitei asked the waiter again, ‘What ingredients do you use?’ The waiter merely laughed, heh-heh, and did not answer. The gentleman deliberately asked once more, ‘The ingredients are probably haiku poets of the Japanese school, are they not?’ The waiter said, ‘Yes, sir. That is why recently even if one goes to Yokohama, they cannot be obtained. I am truly sorry.’” “Ahahaha! So that is the final comic point. It is splendidly funny.” The master had never burst into such hearty laughter before. He laughed so hard that his knees shook, nearly jolting me off. The master paid no attention to that and kept laughing. It appears that, learning he was not the only one who had fallen for Meitei’s Andrea del Sarto trick, he had suddenly become cheerful. “Then, when the two of us went outside from the Western restaurant, Mr. Meitei said to me, very pleased with himself, ‘Well, did it not go smoothly? Was it not amusing to use Tochimenbo as the source of the joke?’ I said, ‘I am filled with admiration,’ and then we parted. But my lunchtime had been delayed, and with an empty stomach I suffered terribly.” “That must have been hard on you.” Only then did the master show sympathy. On this point I had no objection either. The conversation between the two men broke off for a time, and the sound of my throat purring reached their ears.
